common_name: Dolloff Pole Bean (Vermont Heirloom Dry Bean)

planting.note: Wait until soil has warmed past 60F and frost risk has passed, then sow at the base of 6-8 ft fencing for vines to climb.

directions: This pole bean was kept alive for generations by Roy Dolloff of Burke Hollow, Vermont, specifically because it reliably finishes a dry-bean crop even in short, cool Northeast seasons. Give it legume inoculant at planting and sturdy 6-8 ft support, since it is a vigorous climber. Pick some pods young at the salmon-pink shell stage for fresh shelling, or leave the rest to dry down into flat, chestnut-brown beans. Frequent harvesting of the earliest pods keeps the vines producing right up to frost.

common_name: Grandma Nellie's Mushroom Bean (Umami Pole Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably above 60F; provide tall support since vines climb 7-9 feet.

directions: The lineage of this bean traces to a Russian immigrant who gave the seed to Nellie Chernoff in Kamsack, Saskatchewan, who grew it for thirty years before passing it to her granddaughter. It is prized for a savory, almost meaty flavor when the creamy-yellow pods are cooked at about 5 inches long, well before the brown seeds inside mature. Train the long vines up a trellis or pole and pick every few days to keep plants setting new pods. Because it's an early, heavy producer, it's a good choice for gardeners who want fresh beans quickly in a short season.

planting.note: Sow after soil warms to 60F; the short-vined plants tolerate cool nights better than most dry beans.

directions: Plant breeder Carol Deppe developed this bean from Gaucho and her Beefy Resilient Grex specifically to produce well where spring is cold and summer nights dip into the 50s. Expect a mix of growth habits, from true bush to short vines, and a mottled crop of mostly brown seed with some gold or black mixed in, which actually correlates with better yields than a pure color line. Let pods dry hard on the plant until a fingernail can no longer dent the seed, then thresh for a rich, meaty dry bean comparable in yield to Jacob's Cattle or Soldier. Good air circulation and wider row spacing help prevent mold in the humid late season.

planting.note: Direct sow in warm soil; space rows generously to reduce white mold risk in humid weather.

directions: Kenearly is a refinement of the old Maine Yellow Eye strain, selected at the Kentville research station in Nova Scotia for a larger, more uniform yellow eye and more even maturity than its parent. The plump, cream-colored beans can be picked at the shelling stage or left to dry fully on the vine. Avoid working around plants when foliage is wet, since the variety is susceptible to fungal disease in damp conditions, and give it wide spacing for airflow. It is a dependable keeper for winter baked-bean cookery once fully dried.

common_name: Uncle David's Dakota Dessert (Heirloom Buttercup Squash)

planting.note: Direct seed after soil is warm, or save up to 20 days by transplanting started seedlings out after frost.

directions: David Podoll's family has grown and reselected this buttercup for about 70 years, crossing it with Hubbard-type maximas along the way to boost sweetness, vigor, and cold hardiness, which is why he calls it 'the original buttercup.' The green-skinned fruits have thick flesh and small seed cavities, and the family bakes them into pies with no added sweetener needed. Give the sprawling vines plenty of room and a full season of warmth, and expect somewhat bumpy, button-ended fruit typical of the type. It stores well into winter as a dense, all-purpose squash for both savory and dessert uses.

planting.note: Start indoors about three weeks before the last frost and transplant out once danger of frost has passed, since direct sowing germinates unreliably.

directions: This squat, orange F1 mini pumpkin was bred to deliver hull-less, roastable seeds alongside flesh sized for a single pie. Because direct seeding is unreliable for this type, start it indoors and transplant once the weather is settled and warm. It is a heavy nitrogen feeder, so work compost or fertilizer into the bed before setting plants out, and give vines room to ramble. At 2-4 lbs apiece with a thick stubby handle, each fruit is a tidy one-pie portion, and the seeds roast well as a snack.

common_name: Northeaster Pole Bean (Early Flat-Podded Snap Bean)

planting.note: Sow in warm soil at the base of tall fencing; make a second sowing in midsummer for a fall crop before frost.

directions: Also sold under the name Kwintus, this pole bean ripens nearly two weeks ahead of Kentucky Wonder, making it useful where the growing season runs short. Its flattened 7-8 inch pods stay tender and resist getting stringy even when left to grow large, with flavor that actually improves after a quick blanch. Pick thoroughly and often, since leaving overgrown pods on the vine slows new production. For continuous harvest through frost, sow a second round in July or pair it with a later-maturing variety.

common_name: Abenaki Calais Flint Corn (Indigenous Northeast Dry Corn)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil has warmed, feeding heavily with nitrogen; this strain was bred for short, unreliable Northeast seasons.

directions: Developed and selected for generations by the northern Vermont Abenaki, this flint corn was bred specifically to survive brutal Northeast growing seasons, including, by tradition, the catastrophic 1816 'Year Without a Summer.' Ears are long, thin, and cylindrical, carrying even rows of kernels that run in golden yellow, dark maroon, and orange tones, sometimes mixed on the same ear. Grind each color separately if you want to taste how flavor varies between them, or mix for a multicolor cornmeal. As a dry grinding corn it wants a full, warm season and heavy feeding to fill out ears before the first fall frost.

common_name: Madeley Rounded Leaf Kale (English Heirloom Collard-Type Kale)

planting.note: Direct seed in May for summer harvest, or sow in July-August for overwintered plants that resume growth and throw spring shoots.

directions: This English heirloom reached American gardens through Adaptive Seeds via the Heritage Seed Library's Seeds Ambassadors Project, and it is closely related to the old Thousand Headed kale type. Its large, slightly savoyed, rounded leaves look more like a collard than a typical curly kale, but it keeps that distinctive tenderness even on big, mature leaves and through repeated freeze-thaw cycles. It has performed especially well as a winter crop in unheated high tunnels, pushing out productive spring greens once the days lengthen. Shield young plants from flea beetles with row cover, and expect abundant sprouting side shoots after the main leaves are harvested.

planting.note: Sow direct in spring or late summer; the added vigor from its Redbor parentage lets it overwinter and even behave as a short-lived perennial in mild coastal climates.

directions: This farm-original population was created by crossing classic Lacinato with the purple hybrid kale Redbor, layering shades of red, purple, and blue-green over Lacinato's familiar savoyed leaf texture. The cross also added noticeable vigor and cold hardiness, and in milder Pacific Northwest winters some plants will survive to flower and resow themselves the following year. Grow it like any lacinato kale: full sun, steady moisture, and repeated harvest of the lower leaves as the central rosette lengthens upward.

common_name: Winter Red Kale (Cold-Hardy Red Russian Type)

planting.note: Sow in late summer for a fall-through-spring harvest window, or in early spring; plants sweeten noticeably after frost and send up early 'napini' shoots a month ahead of the main leaf harvest.

directions: Winter Red was developed by Pacific Northwest breeder Tim Peters as a more uniformly colored, more cold-hardy improvement on the old Red Russian salad kale, carrying a trace of wild mustard pungency in its sap. It is grown as a tender salad kale rather than a cooking green, with reddish-purple leaves mild enough to eat raw. Fall sowings give a continuous harvest from early autumn through spring, and darker-red 'napini' flower shoots appear about a month before the main leaf crop is ready. Direct sow and thin rather than transplant for best establishment.

common_name: Stocky Golden Roaster Pepper (Thick-Walled Golden Italian)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out only once soil and nights are reliably warm, since fruit wall thickness and smooth skin develop best with steady heat.

directions: Stocky Golden Roaster is a Wild Garden Seed farm original bred for a broad, smooth, thick-walled golden fruit that holds up well over coals or a flame, since its unwrinkled skin slips off cleanly once charred. Early fruits typically reach about 6 inches before later sets taper to a smaller size as the plant keeps flowering through the season. Give it full sun, warm soil, and even moisture; stake or cage plants once they begin loading up with fruit.

common_name: Stoplight Red Pepper (Early Deep Red Bell)

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks ahead of the last frost; this is one of the earlier-ripening bells in the Stoplight series, useful for shorter growing seasons.

directions: Stoplight Red is part of Wild Garden Seed's Stoplight bell series, selected for large, deep red fruit with thick flesh, prominent lobes, and sweet flavor that is also good eaten green before it fully colors. All the Stoplight bells were bred for earlier ripening than typical bell peppers, which is especially useful in the cool, short summers of the Willamette Valley. Give plants full sun and consistent watering, and expect a flush of green fruit early that gradually ripens to deep red through the season.

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant after frost danger passes; thin walls mature faster than thick-walled roasting peppers, so fruit can be picked relatively early.

directions: Yella Bella is the yellow counterpart to Wild Garden Seed's 'Bella Red,' producing crumpled, twisted, thin-walled yellow Italian-type fruit. Because the walls are thinner than a roasting pepper, it suits raw salads or a quick saute better than fire-roasting. The irregular, folded shape makes cross-cut slices especially decorative on a plate. Grow it like other warm-season Capsicum annuum peppers: full sun, consistent water, and staking if the plant becomes top-heavy with fruit.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant after danger of frost; plan for a tall 6-7 foot vine needing sturdy staking or caging.

directions: Estate is a Wild Garden Seed farm original built from three generations of on-farm crossing: Stupice x Homestead was later crossed with the disease-tolerant Peron Sprayless, combining cool-climate reliability with good flavor. The result is a smooth, round, 3 to 3.5 inch fruit with large juice-filled locules and a meaty interior that holds up well for slicing. Vines grow tall, to 6-7 feet, so plan for sturdy staking or a cage system from the start. Give it full sun and even watering through fruit set to avoid cracking on the smooth skin.

planting.note: Start indoors and set out after frost; semi-determinate vines still reach 6-7 feet, so give them support similar to an indeterminate tomato.

directions: Home Stoop crosses the same cold-hardy 'Stupice' used in Estate with 'Homestead,' but is selected to push fruit size up rather than keep it small. Fruits are somewhat flattened and can reach up to 4 inches across, with a cross-section netted with small, juicy locules that makes for a great fresh slicer. Despite being described as semi-determinate, vines still grow 6-7 feet, so stake or cage them as you would an indeterminate variety. Full sun and steady, even watering help the larger fruit size develop without splitting.

planting.note: Start indoors and transplant after frost; the determinate habit and tolerance for cool nights make it a good match for short or marine-influenced growing seasons.

directions: Nebula is a determinate Wild Garden Seed original that fills the gap between its sister varieties, with red, slightly flattened fruit a bit larger than Estate but smaller than Home Stoop. Fascinated locules give the flesh a softer, juicier slice than Estate's firmer texture. It is a heavy yielder bred to perform well under moderate warmth with cool nighttime temperatures, which suits Pacific Northwest and other marine-climate gardens. Because it is determinate, it needs less aggressive staking than the farm's taller indeterminate lines, though a cage still helps keep fruit-laden branches off the ground.

common_name: Tall Dark Sahara Rudbeckia (Burgundy Black-Eyed Susan)

planting.note: Start indoors 4-6 weeks before the last frost, or direct sow once soil has warmed, for long-stemmed burgundy blooms that keep flowering through late summer.

directions: Tall Dark Sahara is a Wild Garden Seed selection out of the 'Sahara' rudbeckia strain, bred for longer stems and more vigorous growth than 'Cherry Brandy,' the original red-toned rudbeckia it descends from. Blooms range from oxblood and maroon to cranberry and mulberry tones, with doubled to semi-doubled petals that give the flowers extra substance for cutting. Plants reach about 32 inches tall, making them a good back-of-border or cut-flower-row candidate. Grow in full sun with average garden water; like most Rudbeckia hirta selections it behaves as an annual or short-lived perennial depending on winter severity.

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in cool weather; the tight, juicy heads need consistent moisture to stay crisp rather than bolt under heat stress.

directions: Buffon d'Glaces is the first commercial release from a long-running Wild Garden Seed breeding project that crossed the heirloom crisphead 'Reine d'Glaces' with the colorful 'Jester' lettuce. It forms tight, juicy 8-inch heads wrapped in ruffled, toothed leaves marked with high-contrast red stripes and splashes over green. Inside, the color carries through as white with pink patterning that can deepen to solid pink in some heads. Grow it like other crispheads: cool soil, even moisture, and harvest promptly once heads firm up, since crisphead types bolt or lose crunch faster than looser lettuce types in sustained heat.

common_name: Sweet Baby Cos Lettuce (Compact Romaine Type)

planting.note: Direct sow or transplant in cool weather at 6-8 inch spacing; the compact habit suits close succession plantings or containers.

directions: Sweet Baby Cos is a Wild Garden Seed farm original developed by crossing 'Concept' with 'Flashy Butter Oak,' resulting in short, dense, compact medium-green heads sized for single servings. A high proportion of the leaves are bite-sized straight off a mature head, with thick blades and crunchy midribs that make good hand-held 'half shell' salad servings. In bright light the leaf tips pick up a slight color tint, a typical sun-stress response in many lettuces. Space plants 6-8 inches apart and keep soil evenly moist, since cos types can turn bitter or bolt quickly if they dry out or hit a late-season heat spike.

common_name: Amere de Berthcourt Apple (French Bittersweet Cider Apple)

planting.note: Plant a bare-root, semi-dwarf grafted tree in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil, siting a midseason-blooming pollinizer nearby since this variety will not set fruit alone.

directions: A nineteenth-century French bittersweet apple grown almost exclusively for hard cider, prized for a fine, sugary flesh that carries a slight bitterness alongside honey and vanilla notes. The tree is unusually prolific and the fruit is strong enough to stand as a single-varietal cider or to add body and tannin when blended with sharper apples. It needs a different midseason-blooming apple nearby to pollinate, and fruit is best pressed within a couple of months of harvest since it stores only briefly.

planting.note: Plant in a warm, sheltered, full-sun spot since this low-chill, early-blooming apricot sets fruit on its own but its early blossoms are vulnerable to spring frost in cooler zones.

directions: An old Persian variety from nineteenth-century Iran whose name translates roughly to 'sugar piece,' valued for exceptionally sweet, plum-tinged white flesh balanced by a touch of acidity. It is self-fertile, vigorous, and begins bearing within a year or two of planting, making it a quick-reward choice for a home orchard in a mild-winter climate. Because it is a low-chill variety and blooms early, summer pruning to keep the canopy around eight feet tall helps manage its vigorous growth and makes harvesting the rose-blushed fruit easier.

planting.note: Plant alongside a different midseason-blooming apple for pollination, and plan to press the fruit soon after an October harvest since it does not store for long.

directions: Introduced in 1872 by nurseryman Legrand of Yvetot in Normandy, Bramtot is a classic bittersweet French cider apple, small and dark red with a tannin load high enough to shape a cider blend on its own. Growers use it for both sweet and dry hard cider as well as pommeau and apple brandy rather than fresh eating. The tree blooms midseason and needs a compatible pollinizer, and because the fruit only keeps three to four weeks after its mid-autumn harvest, it is best pressed promptly.

planting.note: Plant in well-drained soil with a different midseason-blooming pear nearby, since this variety needs cross-pollination to bear fruit.

directions: This pear arose as a bud-mutation sport of the long-popular Duchesse d'Angouleme, discovered in a garden in Dijon, France around 1870, and is grown today for dessert quality slightly ahead of its parent. Its skin carries heavier bronze russeting than the Angouleme pear it sprang from, and the fruit is intended mainly for fresh eating. Grafted onto semi-dwarfing OHxF 333 rootstock, the tree blooms and bears in midseason, needs a differently-timed pear for pollination, and the harvested fruit keeps three months or more in cold storage.

planting.note: Let fruit hang very late into the season for full flavor, and plant a midseason-blooming apple nearby since this variety needs a pollinizer.

directions: A diminutive dessert apple dating to the 1600s in France, Api Etoile became a favorite on Victorian dessert tables for its flattened, star-like silhouette when viewed from the blossom end, slightly larger than the related Lady apple. Picked at peak ripeness it delivers a bold, zesty, grapefruit-like tartness, then mellows into a milder, sweeter apple after a few weeks in storage. It ripens very late in the season, needs cross-pollination from a midseason-blooming variety, and the bright red-blushed fruit is used for fresh eating, cooking, sauce, and cider alike.

planting.note: Site it in full sun partly for the fall foliage display, and pair it with a different midseason-blooming apple for pollination.

directions: A Georgia heirloom dating to the 1800s that pomologist Tom Burford helped bring back into circulation, grown as much for its ornamental qualities as for the fruit itself, with greenish-bronze summer leaves turning a striking orange-red in fall. The apple's flesh carries a reddish tint, and the crisp, tart fruit sweetens somewhat after a month in storage, best suited to cider, sauces, and chutneys rather than fresh eating. It blooms and ripens in midseason and needs a different midseason variety nearby for cross-pollination.

planting.note: Plant with a same-season-blooming apple for pollination and plan to press the fruit soon after harvest, since it stores for only about a month.

directions: First recorded around 1900 in Devon, England, Brown's Cider is a fragrant bittersharp apple grown specifically for its sharply tannic, flavorful juice rather than for the table. The average-sized fruit has dark red skin over pale flesh and ripens late in the season after a midseason bloom. It needs a differently-named but same-timed apple variety nearby to set fruit, and because it keeps barely a month after picking, growers typically press it into cider soon after harvest.

planting.note: Grow on in cool, humid, part-shade conditions with constantly moist but well-drained soil, since this poppy fails outright in heat, drought, or heavy clay.

directions: This Himalayan poppy relative produces clear sky-blue flowers on stems that can reach a yard tall, and this wild Nepalese collection reportedly persists as a true perennial better than many garden hybrids. It is notoriously demanding, requiring cool summers, high humidity, and constant soil moisture, with essentially no tolerance for heat or drought stress. Gardeners outside cool coastal or mountain climates should expect it to perform as a short-lived specialty plant rather than a long-term perennial. It is deer resistant and flowers from spring into early summer.

planting.note: Plant in humus-rich, part-shade soil with reliable moisture; established clumps tolerate far colder winters than its mild island origin would suggest.

directions: Collected on Jeju Island off the Korean coast by Crug Farm, this baneberry forms a tidy clump of glossy foliage topped by fuzzy white bottlebrush flower spikes in late summer. In the wild it was found as a compact plant in a shaded, seasonally dry streambed, but it grows noticeably larger under regular garden moisture. Plant it in part shade with humus-rich soil and expect excellent winter hardiness well beyond what its mild-climate origin implies. It is deer-resistant and helps extend the shade garden's bloom season into fall.

common_name: Rose Queen Dog-Tooth Violet (Mottled-Leaf Fawn Lily)

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in humus-rich, dappled shade in autumn so roots establish well before the rose-pink flowers appear the following spring.

directions: This selection of the European fawn lily produces nodding, rose-pink, reflexed flowers with a warm caramel throat above handsomely mottled leaves in very early spring. Like other erythroniums it behaves as a true spring ephemeral, flowering and resetting its bulb quickly before disappearing for summer. Plant the small bulbs several inches deep in humus-rich, well-drained shade soil in autumn and let the colony naturalize slowly over years. It pairs well with other small woodland bulbs and needs little beyond steady moisture while actively growing.

planting.note: Mount on a damp log or tuck into a mossy rock crevice in full shade with good air movement, mimicking its epiphytic habit in the wild.

directions: This strap-leafed felt fern from China and Taiwan naturally grows sideways across mossy rocks and tree bark rather than forming an upright clump. The narrow, softly textured fronds make it a distinctive low groundcover for a shaded stumpery or rock garden. Give it steady humidity and good drainage rather than conventional garden soil, mounting it on a log or wedging it into a crevice. It stays evergreen but is only reliably hardy in mild winters, so gardeners north of zone 8 should grow it in a protected container.

common_name: China Doll Maidenhair Fern (Dwarf Yunnan Form)

planting.note: Tuck into a shaded, consistently moist rock crevice or woodland edge and give it a dedicated spot, since growth is extremely slow.

directions: This dwarf maidenhair fern, traced to a Yunnan, China collection introduced to cultivation in the 1990s, stays only a few inches tall, making it one of the smallest named forms of an already delicate species. It spreads at the same unhurried pace as its stature suggests, so avoid crowding it among larger shade perennials. Keep the soil evenly moist and the site shaded, since both drought and strong sun quickly brown the fine fronds. It is deer-resistant and well suited to trough gardens or the front edge of a woodland planting.

planting.note: Give it a sheltered part-shade to shaded site with moderate, consistent moisture; container it where winters drop much below the mid-20s Fahrenheit.

directions: Still often sold under its older name Schefflera, this evergreen shrub-to-small-tree has fuzzed, rust-colored new growth blushed purple-pink near the leaves, maturing to a dusty matte dark green. Plant it in part shade to shade with even, moderate moisture, and expect reliable outdoor survival only in mild winter climates. Farther north, grow it as a container specimen that can be moved under cover for winter. It benefits from occasional pinching to maintain a bushy rather than leggy habit.

common_name: Edible Bomarea Vine (Guatemalan Climbing Alstroemeria Relative)

planting.note: Plant tubers in full sun with a sturdy trellis or shrub to climb once frost danger has passed, then let the vine die back to the tuber for winter dormancy.

directions: Possibly the most widely cultivated species in its genus, this Central and South American relative of Alstroemeria twines its way up ten feet or more and bears clusters of bright pink, lime-throated tubular flowers through summer and fall. Historically its starchy tubers have served as a minor food crop in parts of its native range. Give it full sun, something to climb, and moderate moisture during active growth, then allow it to go dormant over winter, especially in containers. This species is distinct from the already-common Bomarea multiflora and is untested in the colder end of its reported hardiness range, so treat it cautiously outside zone 8b and warmer until proven.
